# D043 — Overnight protocol (FROZEN before results), 2026-11-10

Purpose:
- Turn the INDICATIVE results in D041 (expert cache) and D042 (n-gram speculation) into frozen ones.
- Test the upstream rebase, which brings CPU-share and ClassLRU.
- Run the first probes of REAP pruning and MTP.

Runner: `artifacts/night/run.py`, recorded through `bin/run_op`. It is a scripted runner rather than `bin/lab` because it has to sample peak VRAM per arm; that deviation is recorded here.
- Quiet-host rule: no compiles, downloads or Codex processes may run during timed arms. The runner checks this before each arm and records it. If the check fails, the arm waits up to 10 minutes and is then marked `untimed`.
- Settings: greedy decoding, seed 1, `-fa on`, ctx 4096, 128 generated tokens.
- Prompts: `artifacts/traces/in/chat.txt` and `code.txt`.
- Peak VRAM comes from nvidia-smi, polled every 0.5 s.

## E1 — Expert cache vs static at matched budgets (Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M)
Budgets: B ≈ 4, 6, 8 and 10 GB.

| Arm | Engine | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | release-1 | static `--n-cpu-moe K_B` |
| C1 | release-1 | `--n-cpu-moe 48 --moe-cache-mib (B − base)` |
| S2 | up1 | static `K_B` |
| C2 | up1 | cache, cpu-share 0 |
| C3 | up1 | cache, cpu-share 0.9 |

- K_B for 4, 6, 8 and 10 GB is 42, 36, 30 and 24. The cache size is set so that peak VRAM is at most the S1 peak + 3%.
- Order: arms are alternated ABBA across 2 rounds, and each arm is one process per prompt.
- **Accept "cache beats static at B"** only if both conditions hold:
  - median decode ≥ +5% over the same engine's static arm, on both prompts;
  - peak VRAM ≤ static + 3%.
- TTFT (prompt eval ms) is reported, never hidden.
- Engagement: every cache arm must log cache activity. If no cache stats appear in stderr, the arm is invalid.
- Quality: all arms use the same weights, so this measures numeric drift only.
  - Measure KLD against S1 at K=18 with `llama-perplexity --kl-divergence` on 8 chunks of 512 from the existing KL text set.
  - Gate: mean KLD ≤ 0.01, and top-1 agreement ≥ 97%.

## E2 — N-gram speculation on top of the best placement (Qwen3-30B)
- Arms: {static K30, the best E1 cache arm at about 8 GB} × {spec none, `ngram-mod`}.
- Prompts: code rewrite and list repeat (`/no_think`), plus chat. 256 tokens, 2 rounds ABBA.
- Accept only if all three hold:
  - text is identical to spec-none;
  - copy-heavy prompts reach ≥ 1.5×;
  - chat is within −3%.
- `draft_n` must be greater than 0 on the copy-heavy prompts (engagement).

## E3 — REAP-pruned Qwen3-30B (15B total, Q4_K_M, 9.75 GB)
- Arms: REAP at K=0 (all-GPU, if it fits in 16 GB) and at the K needed to fit 8 GB, against full Qwen at the same budgets (best E1 arm).
- Quality: wikitext PPL for both models on the same 8×512 chunks, plus greedy text examples.
- Pruning changes the model, so the D035 KLD gate doesn't apply. This is a **trade-off** result, never "lossless".
- Report the PPL ratio, decode t/s and VRAM.

## E4 — MTP speculative decoding (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B UD-Q4_K_M with MTP heads; engine up0/up1)
- Arms: spec none against `--spec-type draft-mtp` with `--spec-draft-n-max` 2 and 3, at K chosen for about 12 GB and about 8 GB.
- Report acceptance, decode t/s, TTFT and VRAM.
- Accept only if text is identical to spec-none at temp 0 and decode ≥ +10%.

## Not allowed tonight
- Pushing `main`.
- Changing Bash permission rules or the host beyond the D042 perf setting.
- Restarting `euaaa-llm-gpu-1` or Sunshine during measurements. Both are restored at session end, per D002.

def parse_capture(manifest, capture, stats):
    raw = {}

        meta = read(capture/f'{name}.status.json')

            raise ValueError(f'{name} failed: {meta}')
        raw[name] = (capture/f'{name}.stdout').read_text()

    ceilings = bandwidth_ceilings(raw['nvidia'],raw['lscpu'],manifest.get('memory_identity'))
    # Legacy captures MUST be rejected before any tensor/model algebra or output.
    guard_bandwidth(samples,ceilings)
    streams = {}
    if 'cpu-stream' in raw or 'cuda-stream' in raw:
        streams = {d:parse_stream(raw[d+'-stream'],d) for d in ('cpu','cuda')}
        guard_bandwidth({'CPU-stream':streams['cpu'],'CUDA-stream':streams['cuda']},ceilings)
        spreads = {q:summary([r['weight_gbs'] for r in streams['cpu'] if r['threads']==8]) for q in BLOCK}
        cpu = {q:spreads[q]['median'] for q in BLOCK}
        gpu = summary([r['weight_gbs'] for r in streams['cuda']])
    else:
        raise ValueError('legacy perf is not a DRAM measurement; rotating stream captures required')
    h2d = parse_h2d(raw['h2d'])
    bw_h2d = summary([r['gbs'] for r in h2d if r['bytes']>=64*1048576])
    k0,k1 = manifest['cpu_layers']
    sys.path.insert(0,str(ROOT/'cc/moe_planner'))
    import decode_model as dm
    if not 0 <= k0 < k1 <= stats['n_layer'] or not stats.get('tensors'):

    # Reject stale tensor headers rather than silently using planner's equal-layer fallback.
    tensors = [t for t in stats['tensors'] if t['role']=='expert_ffn']
    if not math.isclose(sum(t['bytes'] for t in tensors),stats['expert_bytes'],rel_tol=1e-6):
        raise ValueError('expert tensor byte totals do not match')
    a,b = [dm.traffic(stats,'static',k) for k in (k0,k1)]

    dg = (b['gpu_active_bytes']-a['gpu_active_bytes'])/(gpu['median']*1000)
    times = [parse_bench(raw[f'bench-{k}'],coord=k) for k in (k0,k1)]
    hs = [(v-u-dc-dg)/(k1-k0) for u,v in itertools.product(*times)]
    h = statistics.median(hs)

    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest='mode',required=True)

    plan.add_argument('--image',required=True)
    plan.add_argument('--model',required=True)
    plan.add_argument('--cpu-layers',nargs=2,type=int,required=True)
    plan.add_argument('--memory-channels',type=int)
    plan.add_argument('--memory-rate-mts',type=float)
    plan.add_argument('--out',default=str(OUT/'gpu'))
    parse = sub.add_parser('parse')
    parse.add_argument('--capture',required=True)
    parse.add_argument('--stats',required=True,help='Normalized planner stats with tensors, expert_bytes, nonexpert_bytes')
    parse.add_argument('--out',default=str(OUT/'host-calibration.json'))
    args = p.parse_args()
    try:

            if (args.memory_channels is None) != (args.memory_rate_mts is None):
                raise ValueError('supply both memory channels and DDR rate or neither')
            if args.memory_channels is not None:

            emit(out/'manifest.json',manifest)

lines: +CPU-only analysis of local evidence. Writes are confined to `cc/spec_model/**` and `artifacts/codexSPECM/**`. No planner, engine, calibration or source trace was modified.

+Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M: 48 layers, 128 experts/layer, top_k=8. Each domain has one 64-token decode continuation. Only records with phase `decode` enter the analysis; prefill is excluded. Every decode token must have all layers, exactly eight distinct in-range expert IDs and no duplicate token/layer. Records are ordered by sequence and position, and gaps/sequence boundaries split runs. For each layer and d=1..16, take every overlapping consecutive length-d window (65-d windows/domain), count the union of expert IDs, then average. Overlapping windows are correlated; these are descriptive curves, not independent confidence samples. Pooled curves weight all within-domain windows equally and never concatenate domains. Prose, chat and code are all descriptive here; none estimates a workload acceptance rate. Hashes and run lengths are recorded in `results.json`.
+| d | naive d×8 | prose | chat | code | pooled |

+Let U_l(d) be the layer union mean, B_t the actual full expert tensor bytes, and E=128. Static K offloads the first K expert layers. For each tensor in layer l, active bytes per step = B_t × U_l(d)/E = PL4 single-token bytes × U_l(d)/8. Sum CPU bytes by quantization type for l<K and GPU expert bytes for l≥K. All nonexpert weights are on GPU and read once per step, as dense weight reuse permits; they have no expert union. The CSV also includes a conservative literal whole-GPU scaling sensitivity, multiplying nonexpert bytes by mean(U)/8.
+`T_us(K,d) = Σ_type CPU_bytes(type)/(BW_CPU(type)×1000) + GPU_bytes/(BW_GPU×1000) + K×handoff_us + draft_us + d×extra_us_per_token`

+**a is the observed aggregate accepted/proposed draft fraction on engaged steps**, so the numerator is exactly expected accepted drafts when step length is fixed. Bonus/correction tokens and unengaged ordinary steps are excluded from the main grid. Thus d=1,a=1 is the ordinary PL4 baseline; d=1,a<1 counts only accepted drafts and is not an end-to-end decoder throughput prediction. If a instead means independent conditional prefix survival, expected accepted drafts are `Σ_(i=1..d) a^i`, not a×d. Substitute that numerator (or its implied aggregate fraction) rather than interpreting this grid as that different process. A bonus-token model needs explicit verification-token accounting; no free extra token is credited here.

+Tables assume draft_us=0 and extra_us_per_token=0, once-only expert weight reads within a batch and no new compute/KV bottleneck. All d proposed positions cost traffic even when rejected. Actual rejected-path routing may differ from the observed accepted continuation, especially at a=0.5; this grid holds U(d) fixed as an approximation. Repeated expert execution, output projection arithmetic, attention, activation traffic, KV allocation, drafting and sampling overhead can lower performance. This is a bandwidth forecast, not measured speculative throughput.

+PL4 constants: GPU 285.227 GB/s; CPU Q4_K/Q6_K 35.887 GB/s; handoff 136.641 µs/CPU layer. Q6_K shares Q4_K bandwidth as in PL4. The model retains each layer’s actual Q4_K/Q6_K tensor bytes. No additional 1.02 Q8-reuse multiplier is applied. PL4 has no other identifiable fixed per-step cost; inventing an intercept or adding a measured baseline residual would double-count or refit it.
+| K | ordinary PL4 t/s | CPU ms | GPU ms | handoff ms |

+K=0 is omitted: weights alone are 17691.34 MiB, exceeding the recorded 16303 MiB GPU before KV/runtime buffers. K=18,30,42,48 have measured static precedents (D039). This does not establish their speculative batch buffer fit; the planner must check that separately.
+Each table gives the full requested K×d×a grid. All step components, speedups, whole-GPU scaling sensitivity and break-even acceptance are in `predictions.csv`.
+## D042 check: implied effective mean draft length

+D042 §1 reports rewrite 35.6→85.2 t/s (rounded 2.4×), repeat 35.2→106.6 (rounded 3.0×), all proposed drafts accepted, K=30. The raw PL4 baseline is 35.63 t/s. Invert the a=1 curve. Between adjacent integer lengths, mix step times and token rewards to solve for a two-length mixture; do not linearly interpolate throughput. Relative inversion uses the rounded 2.4×/3.0×; absolute inversion uses 85.2/106.6 t/s directly.
+| trace proxy | workload | relative implied d | absolute implied d |

+This is a consistency check, not independent validation: these three routing continuations are not the D042 rewrite/repeat prompts, and D042 does not report the length distribution or step latencies. Acceptance ≈100% does not mean speculation engages on every step. Ordinary fallback steps or positive draft overhead would generally require longer engaged batches than these idealized effective lengths. A mean alone cannot identify E[U(D)] for a broad distribution. Do not infer observed draft lengths from these inversions. Capture per-step proposed/accepted lengths, target verification time, draft time and engagement alongside D042 timing counters to test the mechanism.

+Use `ngram-mod` as a workload-gated candidate for copying, rewrite/refactor and repeat tasks. Require fit for the model, KV and chosen verification batch. Log draft_n and draft_n_accepted; estimate aggregate a by draft length and the fraction rho of output tokens produced during engaged steps. Open chat in D042 had zero drafts: select no speculative speedup when rho=0. Measure drafting and incremental per-token compute costs rather than assuming they vanish.

+For each feasible d=2..16, compute the worst supplied domain speedup `s(d)=min_domain a(d)×d×T1/[T(d)+draft_us(d)+extra_us_per_token×d]`. Use `S(d)=1/[1-rho+rho/s(d)]` for a token-fraction engagement mixture. Enable only if the best S≥1.10 (an explicit engineering margin), and choose its d as draft_max. Recompute with observed a(d); a fixed acceptance fraction at every d is only the requested sensitivity grid. If the optimum reaches 16, it is the largest evaluated length, not a demonstrated global optimum. Do not extrapolate past 16 from these 64-token traces.
+| K | a | enable | draft_max | worst-domain gain (rho=1, zero extra costs) |

+Treat this as an analytical candidate rule requiring an end-to-end check. Choose the smaller feasible length or disable if measured acceptance, engagement or added compute removes the margin. No existing planner files were changed; `cc/spec_model/model.py:recommend` provides the isolated rule.

+All analysis uses only Python’s standard library. Tests cross-check d=1 against PL4, brute-force real trace unions, sequence/gap handling, type-aware byte accounting, rejection numerator semantics, inversion and lever gates.

def csv_sample(launches):
    stream = io.StringIO()
    writer = csv.writer(stream)
    writer.writerow(['ID', 'Process ID', 'Kernel Name', 'Metric Name', 'Metric Unit', 'Metric Value'])
    for i, (duration, unit, size, byte_unit, dram) in enumerate(launches):
        for metric, metric_unit, value in [(ncu.TIME, unit, duration), (ncu.READ, byte_unit, size),
                                          (ncu.DRAM, '%', dram), (ncu.SM, '%', 2)]:
            writer.writerow([i, 7, 'void example<int>(float *, int)', metric, metric_unit, value])
    return stream.getvalue()

results:
The search turned up an open-source local inference engine called Strata, which is built around MoE models. Sources differ on its hardware requirements, and I didn't find the GitHub repository itself.

- **What it is:** Strata is a specialized engine, mainly for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, that splits MoE expert weights across GPU memory, system RAM, CPU compute, and SSD storage to run the model on consumer GPUs. One source describes it as MIT-licensed and aimed at consumer home PCs.
- **Hardware needs:** One article says a GPU with at least 12GB of VRAM and at least 32GB of main memory is required. A second lists an 8GB+ NVIDIA GPU, and a third mentions 12GB+ VRAM and 64GB RAM. A user report also described a 6GB card failing because the expert cache could not be allocated.
- **Performance claims:** One aggregator reports 60-95 tokens per second. A social-media mention cites about 2200 prefill and 67 decode tokens per second on a single card, but that is an anecdote, not a benchmark.
- **Caveats:** One article says it is best understood as a highly specialized Qwen inference engine rather than a universal replacement for Ollama, llama.cpp or vLLM. Also, a speedup in v0.1.42 depended on a default setting, STRATA_ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP=7, which one source says affects output accuracy unless it is reverted.
- **Not the same project:** The "Stratum" paper (arXiv 2510.05245) is an unrelated academic MoE serving system using 3D-stacked DRAM. Don't confuse it with Strata.

These sources are mostly secondary blogs and aggregators, and the details, especially the Qwen3.8 model naming, should be checked against the official GitHub repository (architectds/Strata) before relying on them.

### Tuning for your PC (`--calibrate`)
Some engine settings depend on the PC more than on the model:
| Setting | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `--pcie-frac` | Share of the experts missing from VRAM that are copied to the GPU instead of computed by the CPU. A fast PCIe link and a slow CPU want more; a laptop's narrow link wants less. |
| `--spec-min-p` | How sure the draft layer must be to add another guess to a check. |
| `--pool-workers` | How many CPU threads compute experts. On CPUs with efficiency cores, fewer can be faster. |
| `--adapt-every`, `--adapt-swaps`, `--adapt-decay` | How busily the VRAM expert cache follows the conversation. A CPU that reads missed experts slowly (DDR3 or DDR4 in few channels) gains from more swaps. |
| `--prefill-pipe` | On two or more cards (layer split), the prompt chunks that keep the cards reading at once. See [MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md). |
The defaults were measured on a Ryzen 5 7600 with an RTX 5070. From a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --calibrate` (Linux: `./setup.sh --calibrate`)
measures output speed with each setting on your PC and keeps one only when it is more than 3% faster. The result is
remembered per PC and model, and updates keep it. Measuring the worker count restarts the model more than once, so the PC
is busy and can stop responding for a minute or two at each restart.
## Memory modes
### KV cache
| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--kv int8` (default) | 8-bit KV cache. |
| `--kv q4_0` | Half the KV memory with a Hadamard rotation before 4-bit rounding. About 4% faster at 128K, measurably less precise on long documents (perplexity +8-12%; needle tests still pass). Setup asks above 8K context. |
| `--kv k8v4` | Keys at 8 bits, values as rotated 4-bit: 23% less KV memory than 8-bit, so more experts fit in VRAM. More precise than `q4_0` on long documents. Prompts are 2-5% slower. |
| `--kv-streaming on\|off\|auto` | Keeps the context's KV cache in RAM and only the part attention reads in VRAM (`--kv-resident 32768`), so more experts fit on the GPU. Costs about 13.7 KB of RAM per context token (1.7 GB at 128K). Setup turns it on from 64K 
| `--kv-grow` (or `STRATA_KV_GROW=1`; `--no-kv-grow` turns it off) | The KV takes VRAM only for the cells the requests reach; the expert cache holds the rest and gives slots back as the context grows. Needs one GPU, an expert profile, the whole KV in VRAM and 
`STRATA_KV_HOST_REGISTER=1` forces the KV host copy to be pinned with `cudaHostRegister` (the order WSL2 uses
automatically); `0` forces `cudaHostAlloc` first.
### Low-RAM modes (chosen by setup)
Normally all of a model's experts are copied into RAM (23-50 GB, pinned) and the GPU holds a copy of the most-used ones.
When the RAM cannot hold them beside the system (the experts plus about 10 GB), setup picks one of these:
| Mode | Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mapped | `--mmap-experts` | Maps the experts from one file in the model's folder (the pack's `experts.bin`, +23-50 GB of disk), or from the GGUF files themselves for native packs that have no `experts.bin`. The OS file cache holds what the GPU does not and c
| Resident | `--resident-experts` | When the experts the GPU does not hold fit the RAM, the engine copies exactly those into RAM at start. Nothing is read from the SSD while it answers. |
| RAM budget | `--resident-budget-gib N` | The N GiB of experts the GPU does not hold that the profile ranks hottest are copied into RAM; the rest are read from the files. Implies `--mmap-experts` and leaves 4 GiB of headroom. On Windows the available commit l
- In a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --setup --low-ram on|off` overrides the choice, and `--low-ram resident|mmap` forces one variant.
- The resident variant keeps 4 GB of the RAM it finds free (`STRATA_RESIDENT_HEADROOM_GIB`). When even the missing experts do
  not fit, it says so and runs the mapped mode. The server log shows per request how many expert reads went to the file
  (`resident RAM: ... blob reads from the file`, 0 in steady use).
- The adaptive tier (`--adapt-every`) keeps following the conversation in the resident mode. `--adapt-async 1` (opt-in,
  `--serve`) moves the swaps between decode windows on a helper thread. With `--batch` slots it works between their
  windows too, but not with `--batch-groups` or `--peer-device`. It is not bit-exact from run to run.
- `STRATA_RAM_ADAPT=<n>` (opt-in, `--serve`, one GPU, needs `--adapt-every`): the RAM copy also follows the conversation.
  A layer swaps up to 4 pairs per window: the experts the windows keep routing to (decayed count 2 or more) take the
  RAM places of unused experts of the same layer (count below 0.5), largest difference first. The incoming expert was
  usually read for the window before; when its blob still sits in that read's stage buffer it is copied from there and
  no file read is made. `n` caps only the pairs that need a file read (`=1` is enough in practice). The log counts how
  many experts moved and how many came out of a stage buffer.
- Several GPUs: setup recommends one GPU in the low-RAM mode and asks. `--gpus 0,1` shares the model across both cards
  ([MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md#using-it)). `--yes` keeps one GPU.
- With a page-locked copy the GPU also takes its share of the misses over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). `--pcie-frac 0` (or
  `STRATA_RESIDENT_PIN=0`) gives the mapped mode's exact tokens.
- Linux, opt-in: `STRATA_ARENA_MMAP=1` maps a native pack's expert arena read-only from `experts.bin` instead of reading
  it into locked RAM (for example 2x 16 GB GPUs with 32 GB of RAM). Run it with `--pcie-frac 0`.
- Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_FILE_RELEASE=1` trims the file-backed pages of experts after their GPU uploads. It is a
  working-set hint, not an unmap, and it does not reduce committed memory or SSD reads
  ([measurements and limits](../bench/results/2026-10-04-windows-mapped-release/README.md)).
- Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_PIN_BY_NEED=1` (arena on one GPU) registers the profile's non-GPU-resident experts by rank up to
  `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` (29 by default on Windows) instead of the first ~30 GiB.
- Windows CUDA keeps 640 MiB then 160 MiB of page-lockable memory free while the arena pins (`STRATA_PIN_RESERVE_MIB=N`, `0`
  turns it off, and it sets the reserve on any OS). If a required buffer is still refused, the error ends with
  `[pinned-memory-exhausted]` and names the `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` to start with.
- `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1` (opt-in): an adaptive swap hands buffer ownership over instead of copying the evicted blob into
  the RAM copy. Same tokens, fewer host copies, about 1.4 GiB more page-locked RAM. See
  [EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md](EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md).
### Linux file tier
When experts are read from GGUF files in place, Linux runs three things by default. Off switches are in brackets.
| Part | Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero-copy | `STRATA_COLD_OVERLAP=4` (`0` = off) | An expert whose three tensors' pages are all in the page cache is computed straight from the mapping, with no staging copy. |
| io prefetch | `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` (`0` = off) | I/O threads read the layer's uncached experts and the router-predicted ones of the next layers with whole-blob `pread`s into the page cache. Tunables: `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_K`, `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH_DEPTH` (2), `S
| Decode gate | `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE=1` (`0` = off) | Every 16 decode windows the read-ahead is judged. It runs only while the page cache has room for the experts (off below 0.55, on above 0.65: `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE_LO` and `_HI`) and while it pays (`STRATA_IO_PF_
For an `experts.bin` pack, io prefetch and the gate switch on when the page cache has room for at least 55% of the experts
(the tightest cgroup limit or `MemAvailable`, asked once at start). Below that the pack reads as before and the log says so;
`STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` forces it. The container RAM check counts a cgroup's clean page cache as available. The startup log
names what is on. When every expert is in the GPU caches (the decode reads nothing from the file tier) the defaults, the decode gate and the routing-aware prefetch are off, and they come back when a request starts with fewer experts held (a VRAM resize, an evi
memory pressure reset the GPU in most runs; with `--adapt-every 100000` there were none, and the cause is not found.
The weights and the MTP draft files are asked for ahead of their reads at start (madvise and `posix_fadvise` WILLNEED, 128 KiB
steps), which matters on a slow drive: `STRATA_READ_AHEAD=0` turns it off, `STRATA_FILL_AHEAD=N` sets how many fill pairs
are requested ahead (default 256).
The prompt chunk follows the host's memory (Linux, file tier, on by default). When the page cache is smaller than the file
set, a planner picks the chunk and ring with the fewest predicted bytes read per prompt from the RAM copy, the page cache that
is left, the drive class and the PCIe link. It prints `chunk 8192 -> 3840, ring 96 -> 96: ...` when it changes the pick and
`chunk 8192 kept: ...` when it does not. It does nothing when the GPU holds every expert, when the file set fits the cache,
and on Windows. `STRATA_PREFILL_HOST_PLAN=0` turns it off; `STRATA_SSD_GBPS` overrides the drive speed;
`--prefill N` and `STRATA_PREFILL_RING` always win.
### Reading the tiers
With `--stats` the engine prints the tiers of the decode (`expert tiers`: blobs from the RAM copy, blobs and MB from the
files, read time; `routing prefetch`: how many file reads had been warmed). The server log has the same per request, and
`GET /metrics` lists `ram_blobs`, `file_blobs`, `file_mb`, `drafts_offered` and `drafts_accepted` per recent request, with
`totals` since the start. `hit_rate` is the VRAM share of the experts looked up; experts the GPU reads over PCIe
(`--pcie-frac`) are not in it, so a higher `--pcie-frac` raises it even when decoding gets slower. `pcie_share` is their
share of all routed experts. The Monitor tab shows both. The request list in the Monitor tab also shows the prompt's own speed: what the cache already held is not read
again, so it is the fresh tokens (`prompt_tokens` minus `reused`) over the prompt time (`prompt_ms`), and a request that read no
new token shows no number.
Profiling: start the server with `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` (and `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1` for the GPU side). After each request
the engine log has a `strata decode timing:` line and a `strata decode GPU stages (ms/window):` line. The GPU profile slows
decoding a little: use it to compare, not to measure speed. `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_STATS=1` scores the next-layer expert
prediction every 100 windows and costs CPU. `tools/replay_cache_policy.py` replays a `--dump-routing` trace through the
adaptive tier's swap policy offline.
In the serial serve loop the timing line lists the wall-time parts in the order they run: `adapt wait + verify +
commit/emit + draft + adapt join + other`. `other` is the decode time minus the named parts, not a step of its own.
The times are host wall times, averaged over every decode window, and the bracketed parts of verify are already inside
verify. The pipelined decode keeps the older line (`ms/window = verify ...`) and batch slots are not covered, so a script
that reads this line must accept `ms/window = adapt wait` for a serial run.
### Draft layer
| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--mtp` | Use the model's MTP draft layer (setup passes it). The server also runs without it: drafts then come from the suffix and prompt-lookup drafter only, every token is still verified, and the draft layer's ~0.7-1 GiB of VRAM goes to the expert cache. |
| `--spec N`, `--spec-min-p P` | Draft depth and the confidence needed to add a guess. Setup's default is `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`. |
| `--draft-vocab en\|cyrillic\|fr` (setup) | The draft layer can only propose tokens from a subset of the vocabulary. The default subset includes every Chinese, Japanese and Korean token. `en` keeps the English and code subset (~110 MiB less VRAM, English 1-2%
| `--lookup-chain-min M`, `--mtp-hnorm stream`, `--mtp-draft-vocab FILE` | Finer controls: the shortest context match `--lookup-chain` extends (default 3), one norm per stream, and a token subset of your own. |
When the start stops with "the draft head does not fit" (a 12 GB card with a long context), the engine says how much it needs
and which smaller subset fits. Setup suggests `--draft-vocab en` on cards under 14 GB; nothing changes unless you pass it.
**Reproducible output.** With the IQ models the CPU rounds one-token expert groups and multi-token groups differently, so the
same prompt at temperature 0 can end in a different, equally good answer when drafting, cache state or a resumed conversation
differ. `STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1` uses the multi-token kernels for every group, so the answer no longer depends on drafting (IQ3_S
decode -1 to -3% on a Ryzen 7600). For byte-identical repeats also add `--prompt-cache 0 --adapt-swaps 0 --pcie-frac 0` to
the engine args. `--pcie-frac 0` costs decode speed, so keep it for A/B runs.
---
### The expert cache size is a budget
`--expert-cache N` (`"expert_cache": N`) is `N` times the largest expert blob. The engine compares it only with the free VRAM
it reads before the slots are written. `--expert-cache auto` (the default) checks again once the slots are written and
shrinks if they do not fit. Under Windows an over-sized fixed cache does not fail. The driver pages the excess to system
memory, the start looks normal, and only the speed collapses (see the history table for one measurement).
- The startup line `... MiB of VRAM free with everything loaded` is the tell. Below about 256 MiB it adds
  `LOW: requests may stall; add --vram-reserve-mib N` with the value that would have left room.
- Keep the cache on `auto`, or keep an explicit size and raise `--vram-reserve-mib`, which the engine deducts before it sizes
  the cache.
- That figure is read before the verify windows are captured, so it moves down by tens of MiB per captured window or `--batch`
  layout. Each request re-reads the free VRAM and prints `WARNING: only N MiB of VRAM free at the start of this request` below
  1 GiB on Windows (512 MiB elsewhere), with the `--vram-reserve-mib` that would leave room. The fix is a larger
  `--vram-reserve-mib`, a smaller `--max-context` or `--batch`, or the NVIDIA setting `CUDA - Sysmem Fallback Policy` set to
  `Prefer No Sysmem Fallback` for the engine's executable.
- Performance Monitor's `GPU Process Memory` counters did not separate fast from slow runs because they count deliberately
  pinned memory. Use the free line in the log.
- A stall named "request" can be the OS paging the engine's own memory while it parks the outgoing conversation (the stage
  reads `request: parking the previous conversation`). The cure is memory: a smaller `--resident-budget-gib`, a smaller
  `--conversation-cache-mib`, or the pagefile on an SSD.
---
### Conversation cache
A request that continues a chat reads only the part after what the engine already holds: the live session, or one of the
checkpoints in RAM (up to 6, about 118 MB each, taken at the start of each new assistant turn and every 16K prompt tokens). A
checkpoint is used only when the prompt starts with exactly its tokens and pictures. The oldest checkpoint, in practice
the end of the system prompt that every chat of a client shares, is kept for good, so a new chat that shares the prefix
starts after it. A prompt of 2,048 tokens or more is also checkpointed at the end of its system prompt. Claude Code stamps its
system prompt with a billing header that changes on every request; the server pins both stamps so the prompt stays the same.
| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--prompt-cache N` | Number of checkpoints (`0` = off, which also disables parking). |
| `--prompt-cache-every N`, `--prompt-cache-root N`, `--turn-token ID` | Checkpoint interval, the system-prompt checkpoint (`0` = none) and the turn token. The interval is not a piece-size setting: [what it does](PROMPT_CACHE_TAIL.md#--prompt-cache-every-does-
| `--prompt-cache-spread` (opt-in) | The checkpoint that leaves is the one whose removal leaves the smallest gap, so the kept points thin out geometrically back from the end. An agent that rewrites its history a few thousand tokens back then resumes near the e
| `"strata_checkpoint": false` (per request) | A one-shot request that no later request continues saves no checkpoints and keeps no session. |
| `"strata_prefix": {"messages": 1}` (per request, opt-in) | One long document, many questions. Marks where the document ends: `{"messages": 1}`, `{"message": 0, "chars": 210000}` or `{"tokens": 12345}`. The checkpoint at the boundary is pinned, so 20 question
| `--conversation-cache-mib N`, `--conversation-cache-slots N` | Park conversations in a bounded host-RAM cache so alternating requests (controller and worker histories, sub-agents) reuse their prompts. Without `--conversation-cache-mib` the budget is 40% of t
| `--conversation-cache-min-tokens N` | Park only conversations of at least N tokens, so short side requests do not evict a long conversation. Default `0` (park all). |
| `--conversation-cache-park-gain N` (opt-in) | Park a conversation again only after it advanced N tokens past the copy it would replace. |
| `--conversation-cache-min-free-mib N` | RAM floor, default 2560. Parking and session files are skipped when less than the snapshot plus the floor is available. |
| `--memory-limit-mib N` (or `STRATA_MEMORY_LIMIT_MIB`) | Total RAM this engine's container may use, for when a container cannot see its own limit. Config `args`: `"--memory-limit-mib", "102400"`. `0` = none. |
The RAM figure the floor is checked against is the smallest of `MemAvailable`, the room under each cgroup limit visible to
the engine (v2 `memory.max` and `memory.high`, v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes`, less clean inactive file cache) and the
`--memory-limit-mib` cap. The startup line `strata generate: memory guard: limit X GiB (source: flag|cgroup|meminfo) ...` names
the source. It covers parking and session files only, not the startup sizing of the arena, the resident budget or the Windows commit check.
**When the arena does not fit in the RAM that is free (#4051).** The engine checks the RAM before it reads the experts into the
arena. A memory limit below the arena (a container) stops the start with the numbers. Less free RAM than the arena (an engine
that was still exiting, another program) is waited for up to 20 s, and the log says so (`STRATA_ARENA_RAM_WAIT_S` changes the
seconds, `0` loads at once). On Linux, if free memory, file cache or a reserved huge-page pool can hold the experts, they load anyway with a warning; otherwise the run reads them from the file. `STRATA_ARENA_FILE_CACHE=0` always reads from the file. Below half
of the arena the warning adds that the whole PC can stall in memory reclaim, and that a systemd `MemoryHigh=` below the RAM keeps
one program from taking all of it. The server, before it starts an engine, ends one that an earlier run left behind and now waits up
to 120 s for it to be gone (it used to wait 10 s): an engine with tens of GB of pinned memory needs longer to give it back, and the
next one started beside it ran the PC out of RAM (#4051).
**When it is still short after the wait: the RAM copy, and `--ram-keep-gib` (R5070).** The arena is used only when it fits. When it does
not (#4846), the engine does not read every expert through the file any more: with a static expert profile it keeps the hottest experts
in a RAM copy, as much as the RAM available at the start allows after a headroom, and reads the rest from the model files (the
`--resident-budget-gib` form). On a 12 GB card with a 63 GB PC and 44.6 GiB available this took IQ3_S at 128K from 9.4 to 25-28 tok/s.
- `--ram-keep-gib W` (default 0; `STRATA_RAM_KEEP_GIB` is the same for a program that cannot pass the flag) is the RAM you want left free
  for your own work. It covers both decisions: the arena is used only if W GiB are still available after it, and the RAM copy that
  replaces it leaves `max(W, the safety headroom)` free. The arena needs `arena + one blob + W` available; the log says so
  ("the expert arena needs ... with the W GiB --ram-keep-gib asks to leave free").
- The safety headroom is 8 GiB on Windows and 4 GiB elsewhere. It is not a preference: on Windows the copy is read through a mapped view
  whose pages count against the process until the engine gives them back (every 4 layers), and with less than 8 GiB of room available RAM
  fell to 0.9 GiB during the copy. `STRATA_RESIDENT_HEADROOM_GIB`, when set, decides the headroom instead of both (testers).

### Tuning for your PC (`--calibrate`)
Some engine settings depend on the PC more than on the model:
| Setting | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| `--pcie-frac` | Share of the experts missing from VRAM that are copied to the GPU instead of computed by the CPU. A fast PCIe link and a slow CPU want more; a laptop's narrow link wants less. |
| `--spec-min-p` | How sure the draft layer must be to add another guess to a check. |
| `--pool-workers` | How many CPU threads compute experts. On CPUs with efficiency cores, fewer can be faster. |
| `--adapt-every`, `--adapt-swaps`, `--adapt-decay` | How busily the VRAM expert cache follows the conversation. A CPU that reads missed experts slowly (DDR3 or DDR4 in few channels) gains from more swaps. |
| `--prefill-pipe` | On two or more cards (layer split), the prompt chunks that keep the cards reading at once. See [MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md). |
The defaults were measured on a Ryzen 5 7600 with an RTX 5070. From a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --calibrate` (Linux: `./setup.sh --calibrate`)
measures output speed with each setting on your PC and keeps one only when it is more than 3% faster. The result is
remembered per PC and model, and updates keep it. Measuring the worker count restarts the model more than once, so the PC
is busy and can stop responding for a minute or two at each restart.
## Memory modes
### KV cache
| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--kv int8` (default) | 8-bit KV cache. |
| `--kv q4_0` | Half the KV memory with a Hadamard rotation before 4-bit rounding. About 4% faster at 128K, measurably less precise on long documents (perplexity +8-12%; needle tests still pass). Setup asks above 8K context. |
| `--kv k8v4` | Keys at 8 bits, values as rotated 4-bit: 23% less KV memory than 8-bit, so more experts fit in VRAM. More precise than `q4_0` on long documents. Prompts are 2-5% slower. |
| `--kv-streaming on\|off\|auto` | Keeps the context's KV cache in RAM and only the part attention reads in VRAM (`--kv-resident 32768`), so more experts fit on the GPU. Costs about 13.7 KB of RAM per context token (1.7 GB at 128K). Setup turns it on from 64K 
| `--kv-grow` (or `STRATA_KV_GROW=1`; `--no-kv-grow` turns it off) | The KV takes VRAM only for the cells the requests reach; the expert cache holds the rest and gives slots back as the context grows. Needs one GPU, an expert profile, the whole KV in VRAM and 
`STRATA_KV_HOST_REGISTER=1` forces the KV host copy to be pinned with `cudaHostRegister` (the order WSL2 uses
automatically); `0` forces `cudaHostAlloc` first.
### Low-RAM modes (chosen by setup)
Normally all of a model's experts are copied into RAM (23-50 GB, pinned) and the GPU holds a copy of the most-used ones.
When the RAM cannot hold them beside the system (the experts plus about 10 GB), setup picks one of these:
| Mode | Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mapped | `--mmap-experts` | Maps the experts from one file in the model's folder (the pack's `experts.bin`, +23-50 GB of disk), or from the GGUF files themselves for native packs that have no `experts.bin`. The OS file cache holds what the GPU does not and c
| Resident | `--resident-experts` | When the experts the GPU does not hold fit the RAM, the engine copies exactly those into RAM at start. Nothing is read from the SSD while it answers. |
| RAM budget | `--resident-budget-gib N` | The N GiB of experts the GPU does not hold that the profile ranks hottest are copied into RAM; the rest are read from the files. Implies `--mmap-experts` and leaves 4 GiB of headroom. On Windows the available commit l
- In a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --setup --low-ram on|off` overrides the choice, and `--low-ram resident|mmap` forces one variant.
- The resident variant keeps 4 GB of the RAM it finds free (`STRATA_RESIDENT_HEADROOM_GIB`). When even the missing experts do
  not fit, it says so and runs the mapped mode. The server log shows per request how many expert reads went to the file
  (`resident RAM: ... blob reads from the file`, 0 in steady use).
- The adaptive tier (`--adapt-every`) keeps following the conversation in the resident mode. `--adapt-async 1` (opt-in,
  `--serve`) moves the swaps between decode windows on a helper thread. With `--batch` slots it works between their
  windows too, but not with `--batch-groups` or `--peer-device`. It is not bit-exact from run to run.
- `STRATA_RAM_ADAPT=<n>` (opt-in, `--serve`, one GPU, needs `--adapt-every`): the RAM copy also follows the conversation.
  A layer swaps up to 4 pairs per window: the experts the windows keep routing to (decayed count 2 or more) take the
  RAM places of unused experts of the same layer (count below 0.5), largest difference first. The incoming expert was
  usually read for the window before; when its blob still sits in that read's stage buffer it is copied from there and
  no file read is made. `n` caps only the pairs that need a file read (`=1` is enough in practice). The log counts how
  many experts moved and how many came out of a stage buffer.
- Several GPUs: setup recommends one GPU in the low-RAM mode and asks. `--gpus 0,1` shares the model across both cards
  ([MULTI_GPU.md](MULTI_GPU.md#using-it)). `--yes` keeps one GPU.
- With a page-locked copy the GPU also takes its share of the misses over PCIe (`--pcie-frac`). `--pcie-frac 0` (or
  `STRATA_RESIDENT_PIN=0`) gives the mapped mode's exact tokens.
- Linux, opt-in: `STRATA_ARENA_MMAP=1` maps a native pack's expert arena read-only from `experts.bin` instead of reading
  it into locked RAM (for example 2x 16 GB GPUs with 32 GB of RAM). Run it with `--pcie-frac 0`.
- Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_FILE_RELEASE=1` trims the file-backed pages of experts after their GPU uploads. It is a
  working-set hint, not an unmap, and it does not reduce committed memory or SSD reads
  ([measurements and limits](../bench/results/2026-10-04-windows-mapped-release/README.md)).
- Windows, opt-in: `STRATA_PIN_BY_NEED=1` (arena on one GPU) registers the profile's non-GPU-resident experts by rank up to
  `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` (29 by default on Windows) instead of the first ~30 GiB.
- Windows CUDA keeps 640 MiB then 160 MiB of page-lockable memory free while the arena pins (`STRATA_PIN_RESERVE_MIB=N`, `0`
  turns it off, and it sets the reserve on any OS). If a required buffer is still refused, the error ends with
  `[pinned-memory-exhausted]` and names the `STRATA_ARENA_PIN_GIB` to start with.
- `STRATA_EXCHANGE_ROTATE=1` (opt-in): an adaptive swap hands buffer ownership over instead of copying the evicted blob into
  the RAM copy. Same tokens, fewer host copies, about 1.4 GiB more page-locked RAM. See
  [EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md](EXCHANGE_ROTATION.md).
### Linux file tier
When experts are read from GGUF files in place, Linux runs three things by default. Off switches are in brackets.
| Part | Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero-copy | `STRATA_COLD_OVERLAP=4` (`0` = off) | An expert whose three tensors' pages are all in the page cache is computed straight from the mapping, with no staging copy. |
| io prefetch | `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` (`0` = off) | I/O threads read the layer's uncached experts and the router-predicted ones of the next layers with whole-blob `pread`s into the page cache. Tunables: `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_K`, `STRATA_IO_PREFETCH_DEPTH` (2), `S
| Decode gate | `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE=1` (`0` = off) | Every 16 decode windows the read-ahead is judged. It runs only while the page cache has room for the experts (off below 0.55, on above 0.65: `STRATA_IO_PF_GATE_LO` and `_HI`) and while it pays (`STRATA_IO_PF_
For an `experts.bin` pack, io prefetch and the gate switch on when the page cache has room for at least 55% of the experts
(the tightest cgroup limit or `MemAvailable`, asked once at start). Below that the pack reads as before and the log says so;
`STRATA_IO_PREFETCH=1` forces it. The container RAM check counts a cgroup's clean page cache as available. The startup log
names what is on. When every expert is in the GPU caches (the decode reads nothing from the file tier) the defaults, the decode gate and the routing-aware prefetch are off, and they come back when a request starts with fewer experts held (a VRAM resize, an evi
memory pressure reset the GPU in most runs; with `--adapt-every 100000` there were none, and the cause is not found.
The weights and the MTP draft files are asked for ahead of their reads at start (madvise and `posix_fadvise` WILLNEED, 128 KiB
steps), which matters on a slow drive: `STRATA_READ_AHEAD=0` turns it off, `STRATA_FILL_AHEAD=N` sets how many fill pairs
are requested ahead (default 256).
The prompt chunk follows the host's memory (Linux, file tier, on by default). When the page cache is smaller than the file
set, a planner picks the chunk and ring with the fewest predicted bytes read per prompt from the RAM copy, the page cache that
is left, the drive class and the PCIe link. It prints `chunk 8192 -> 3840, ring 96 -> 96: ...` when it changes the pick and
`chunk 8192 kept: ...` when it does not. It does nothing when the GPU holds every expert, when the file set fits the cache,
and on Windows. `STRATA_PREFILL_HOST_PLAN=0` turns it off; `STRATA_SSD_GBPS` overrides the drive speed;
`--prefill N` and `STRATA_PREFILL_RING` always win.
### Reading the tiers
With `--stats` the engine prints the tiers of the decode (`expert tiers`: blobs from the RAM copy, blobs and MB from the
files, read time; `routing prefetch`: how many file reads had been warmed). The server log has the same per request, and
`GET /metrics` lists `ram_blobs`, `file_blobs`, `file_mb`, `drafts_offered` and `drafts_accepted` per recent request, with
`totals` since the start. `hit_rate` is the VRAM share of the experts looked up; experts the GPU reads over PCIe
(`--pcie-frac`) are not in it, so a higher `--pcie-frac` raises it even when decoding gets slower. `pcie_share` is their
share of all routed experts. The Monitor tab shows both. The request list in the Monitor tab also shows the prompt's own speed: what the cache already held is not read
again, so it is the fresh tokens (`prompt_tokens` minus `reused`) over the prompt time (`prompt_ms`), and a request that read no
new token shows no number.
Profiling: start the server with `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING=1` (and `STRATA_VERIFY_PROFILE=1` for the GPU side). After each request
the engine log has a `strata decode timing:` line and a `strata decode GPU stages (ms/window):` line. The GPU profile slows
decoding a little: use it to compare, not to measure speed. `STRATA_LOOKAHEAD_STATS=1` scores the next-layer expert
prediction every 100 windows and costs CPU. `tools/replay_cache_policy.py` replays a `--dump-routing` trace through the
adaptive tier's swap policy offline.
In the serial serve loop the timing line lists the wall-time parts in the order they run: `adapt wait + verify +
commit/emit + draft + adapt join + other`. `other` is the decode time minus the named parts, not a step of its own.
The times are host wall times, averaged over every decode window, and the bracketed parts of verify are already inside
verify. The pipelined decode keeps the older line (`ms/window = verify ...`) and batch slots are not covered, so a script
that reads this line must accept `ms/window = adapt wait` for a serial run.
### Draft layer
| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--mtp` | Use the model's MTP draft layer (setup passes it). The server also runs without it: drafts then come from the suffix and prompt-lookup drafter only, every token is still verified, and the draft layer's ~0.7-1 GiB of VRAM goes to the expert cache. |
| `--spec N`, `--spec-min-p P` | Draft depth and the confidence needed to add a guess. Setup's default is `--spec 4 --spec-min-p 0.5`. |
| `--draft-vocab en\|cyrillic\|fr` (setup) | The draft layer can only propose tokens from a subset of the vocabulary. The default subset includes every Chinese, Japanese and Korean token. `en` keeps the English and code subset (~110 MiB less VRAM, English 1-2%
| `--lookup-chain-min M`, `--mtp-hnorm stream`, `--mtp-draft-vocab FILE` | Finer controls: the shortest context match `--lookup-chain` extends (default 3), one norm per stream, and a token subset of your own. |
When the start stops with "the draft head does not fit" (a 12 GB card with a long context), the engine says how much it needs
and which smaller subset fits. Setup suggests `--draft-vocab en` on cards under 14 GB; nothing changes unless you pass it.
**Reproducible output.** With the IQ models the CPU rounds one-token expert groups and multi-token groups differently, so the
same prompt at temperature 0 can end in a different, equally good answer when drafting, cache state or a resumed conversation
differ. `STRATA_IQ_MT_MIN=1` uses the multi-token kernels for every group, so the answer no longer depends on drafting (IQ3_S
decode -1 to -3% on a Ryzen 7600). For byte-identical repeats also add `--prompt-cache 0 --adapt-swaps 0 --pcie-frac 0` to
the engine args. `--pcie-frac 0` costs decode speed, so keep it for A/B runs.
---
### The expert cache size is a budget
`--expert-cache N` (`"expert_cache": N`) is `N` times the largest expert blob. The engine compares it only with the free VRAM
it reads before the slots are written. `--expert-cache auto` (the default) checks again once the slots are written and
shrinks if they do not fit. Under Windows an over-sized fixed cache does not fail. The driver pages the excess to system
memory, the start looks normal, and only the speed collapses (see the history table for one measurement).
- The startup line `... MiB of VRAM free with everything loaded` is the tell. Below about 256 MiB it adds
  `LOW: requests may stall; add --vram-reserve-mib N` with the value that would have left room.
- Keep the cache on `auto`, or keep an explicit size and raise `--vram-reserve-mib`, which the engine deducts before it sizes
  the cache.
- That figure is read before the verify windows are captured, so it moves down by tens of MiB per captured window or `--batch`
  layout. Each request re-reads the free VRAM and prints `WARNING: only N MiB of VRAM free at the start of this request` below
  1 GiB on Windows (512 MiB elsewhere), with the `--vram-reserve-mib` that would leave room. The fix is a larger
  `--vram-reserve-mib`, a smaller `--max-context` or `--batch`, or the NVIDIA setting `CUDA - Sysmem Fallback Policy` set to
  `Prefer No Sysmem Fallback` for the engine's executable.
- Performance Monitor's `GPU Process Memory` counters did not separate fast from slow runs because they count deliberately
  pinned memory. Use the free line in the log.
- A stall named "request" can be the OS paging the engine's own memory while it parks the outgoing conversation (the stage
  reads `request: parking the previous conversation`). The cure is memory: a smaller `--resident-budget-gib`, a smaller
  `--conversation-cache-mib`, or the pagefile on an SSD.
---
### Conversation cache
A request that continues a chat reads only the part after what the engine already holds: the live session, or one of the
checkpoints in RAM (up to 6, about 118 MB each, taken at the start of each new assistant turn and every 16K prompt tokens). A
checkpoint is used only when the prompt starts with exactly its tokens and pictures. The oldest checkpoint, in practice
the end of the system prompt that every chat of a client shares, is kept for good, so a new chat that shares the prefix
starts after it. A prompt of 2,048 tokens or more is also checkpointed at the end of its system prompt. Claude Code stamps its
system prompt with a billing header that changes on every request; the server pins both stamps so the prompt stays the same.
| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--prompt-cache N` | Number of checkpoints (`0` = off, which also disables parking). |
| `--prompt-cache-every N`, `--prompt-cache-root N`, `--turn-token ID` | Checkpoint interval, the system-prompt checkpoint (`0` = none) and the turn token. The interval is not a piece-size setting: [what it does](PROMPT_CACHE_TAIL.md#--prompt-cache-every-does-
| `--prompt-cache-spread` (opt-in) | The checkpoint that leaves is the one whose removal leaves the smallest gap, so the kept points thin out geometrically back from the end. An agent that rewrites its history a few thousand tokens back then resumes near the e
| `"strata_checkpoint": false` (per request) | A one-shot request that no later request continues saves no checkpoints and keeps no session. |

The RAM figure the floor is checked against is the smallest of `MemAvailable`, the room under each cgroup limit visible to
the engine (v2 `memory.max` and `memory.high`, v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes`, less clean inactive file cache) and the
`--memory-limit-mib` cap. The startup line `strata generate: memory guard: limit X GiB (source: flag|cgroup|meminfo) ...` names
the source. It covers parking and session files only, not the startup sizing of the arena, the resident budget or the Windows commit check.
**When the arena does not fit in the RAM that is free (#4051).** The engine checks the RAM before it reads the experts into the
arena. A memory limit below the arena (a container) stops the start with the numbers. Less free RAM than the arena (an engine
that was still exiting, another program) is waited for up to 20 s, and the log says so (`STRATA_ARENA_RAM_WAIT_S` changes the
seconds, `0` loads at once). On Linux, if free memory, file cache or a reserved huge-page pool can hold the experts, they load anyway with a warning; otherwise the run reads them from the file. `STRATA_ARENA_FILE_CACHE=0` always reads from the file. Below half
of the arena the warning adds that the whole PC can stall in memory reclaim, and that a systemd `MemoryHigh=` below the RAM keeps
one program from taking all of it. The server, before it starts an engine, ends one that an earlier run left behind and now waits up
to 120 s for it to be gone (it used to wait 10 s): an engine with tens of GB of pinned memory needs longer to give it back, and the
next one started beside it ran the PC out of RAM (#4051).
**When it is still short after the wait: the RAM copy, and `--ram-keep-gib` (R5070).** The arena is used only when it fits. When it does
not (#4846), the engine does not read every expert through the file any more: with a static expert profile it keeps the hottest experts
in a RAM copy, as much as the RAM available at the start allows after a headroom, and reads the rest from the model files (the
`--resident-budget-gib` form). On a 12 GB card with a 63 GB PC and 44.6 GiB available this took IQ3_S at 128K from 9.4 to 25-28 tok/s.
- `--ram-keep-gib W` (default 0; `STRATA_RAM_KEEP_GIB` is the same for a program that cannot pass the flag) is the RAM you want left free
  for your own work. It covers both decisions: the arena is used only if W GiB are still available after it, and the RAM copy that
  replaces it leaves `max(W, the safety headroom)` free. The arena needs `arena + one blob + W` available; the log says so
  ("the expert arena needs ... with the W GiB --ram-keep-gib asks to leave free").
- The safety headroom is 8 GiB on Windows and 4 GiB elsewhere. It is not a preference: on Windows the copy is read through a mapped view
  whose pages count against the process until the engine gives them back (every 4 layers), and with less than 8 GiB of room available RAM
  fell to 0.9 GiB during the copy. `STRATA_RESIDENT_HEADROOM_GIB`, when set, decides the headroom instead of both (testers).
- With W = 0 nothing about the fallback changes: the full system is used, the arena whenever it fits, with no margin, and the copy leaves
  the safety headroom. The explicit modes (`--resident-budget-gib N`, `--resident-experts`) leave `max(W, their own 4 GiB)`.
- The app's "Leave 20% for my work" passes W = clamp(ceil(0.2 x RAM in GB), 5, 8) as `STRATA_RAM_KEEP_GIB` in the run config's env (not as the flag, so an older engine chosen in the Engine tab, which ignores an env variable, still starts); `strata serve` and f
- `STRATA_ARENA_FALLBACK_RESIDENT=0` keeps the plain file source for the fallback (testers).
Snapshots hold running state, checkpoints, used K/V pages and draft-layer K/V. They add host RAM, not VRAM. Oldest parked entries
are evicted first. A new conversation that starts at a checkpoint inside a parked one (sub-agents that share a system prompt)
restores that prefix and leaves the parked conversation in place (the log says "borrowed"). Oversized snapshots or host
allocation failures fall back to ordinary prompt processing. With `--layer-split` a parked conversation holds one image per
stage. Parked snapshots are not kept across restarts; session files are. `STRATA_SNAPSHOT_FULL_CAPTURE=1` disables K/V
retention for diagnostics. The Monitor tab's **Conversation cache** card shows parked, restored and evicted counts and the
prompt tokens the cache gave back; `/metrics` has the same under `"conversation_cache"`.

## Experimental speed projection (experimental, off by default)
This is an experiment. It ships with Strata and stays off unless you turn it on. It is a 480 KB control vector for the original
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (`data/experimental-speed-projection/`, not Swift 1.5). After each of layers 4-44 the engine removes one
direction from every hyper-connection stream: `h -= (h . v) v`.
**What it changes.** The vector's package describes it as a **refusal-direction projection**. With it the model declines far fewer
requests, and removing refusals removes a safety behavior, so you are responsible for what the model writes with it on. It also
shifts ordinary answers a little and costs 0.2-0.4% per token. What a chat's tokens/s does depends on the text, so measure it on
your own prompts. The Monitor marks every request ESP or stock.
**Turning it on.** In a source checkout, `START-HERE.bat --setup` asks "Turn on the experimental speed projection?" (default no), or pass
`--experimental-speed-projection on` (`off`, or a path to another vector GGUF). It writes these engine flags into `strata-<model>.json`:
```
--control-vector-scaled <Strata>\data\experimental-speed-projection\Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-experimental-speed-projection.gguf:1.0
--control-vector-layer-range 4 44 --cvec-mode project --cvec-dir per-layer
```
The engine log then says `control vector mode = project, dir = per-layer, layers 4..44 (41 steered)`. A loaded vector is on for
every request unless it says otherwise: Chat settings has a switch, and the API takes `"experimental_speed_projection": false`
(config default: `"sampling": {"experimental_speed_projection": false}`). Switching drops the conversation cache once. Switched
off, the output is token for token the stock model's.

## How it works
<p align="center"><img src="paper/tiers.svg" width="760" alt="memory tiers"></p>
- **GPU (VRAM):** attention and DeltaNet mixers, the gated-residual weights, routers, shared experts, the output head, the MTP draft
  layer, the KV cache (from 64K only its most-read part; the rest streams from RAM) and an **expert cache** that fills the rest of
  VRAM with the most-used experts and adapts to the conversation.
- **RAM:** all 24,576 experts, pinned. The CPU computes the experts that are not on the GPU in place, at the same time as the GPU
  works on the cached ones (AVX-512 and AVX2 kernels, ggml's for the i-quants).
- **SSD:** the 28.8 GB n-gram table, a few rows per token, read unbuffered past the OS cache (`--ple-io direct`). The engine reads the
  table in the format the GGUF has it: IQ4_NL (the default table), Q4_0, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, FP8 (E4M3 with a scale) or BF16. Setup does not
  offer another table.
- **Speculation:** the model's own MTP layer drafts up to 3 tokens and one pass over all 48 layers checks them, for 2.4-3.2 tokens
  per pass on average. When the reply repeats the context (code edits, quoted text), prompt lookup drafts up to 5 tokens from the
  earlier copy, but only where its measured acceptance and cost say it pays. Drafts are checked like the MTP's, so the output is the
  same.
- **Prompts** are processed in chunks of up to 8,192 tokens (`--prefill auto`; 32,768 opt-in) with the experts streamed to the GPU
  over PCIe. The streamed ring is sized in bytes for the pack, and `--prefill auto` picks the largest chunk that keeps that ring
  full. `STRATA_RING_BYTES=0` restores the earlier ring, loan and chunk choice.
The full story, with measurements, bottlenecks and what comes next: **[docs/paper/Strata-Paper.pdf](paper/Strata-Paper.pdf)**.

from pathlib import Path
p=Path('TOOLKIT.md'); t=p.read_text()
sec='''
## Gap audit vs. Strata (MoE-specialised engine, Niko1221/Strata, 2026-11-10)
Source: the Strata README and `docs/DETAILS.md`, read 2026-11-10. Strata runs a 125B MoE on a 12–16 GB card plus host RAM.
Each row is an engine feature, followed by what we have and the gap in tools or levers. P = priority for our goal (memory ↓, accuracy ≈, load/TTFT/decode).

| # | Strata feature | Ours today | Gap (tool / lever) | P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G1 | Three-tier expert store: VRAM cache, pinned RAM, mmap/SSD with `--resident-budget-gib` (hottest-by-profile in RAM) | Planner budgets **VRAM only** and assumes all experts sit in RAM | Host-RAM budget in the planner; mmap/`--no-mmap`/mlock lever; SSD tier cost model; a page-cache-cold run mode | 1 |
| G2 | Load time treated as a feature: madvise/fadvise WILLNEED, startup memory guard | Nothing. "Load time" is in the goal, but there is no tool | Load-time probe: cold (drop caches needs sudo) vs warm page cache, mmap vs no-mmap, time to first token from process start | 1 |
| G3 | Workload realism: a coding-agent conversation (100K start + 8 turns), short-prompt TTFT, long-context decode | 128-token chat/code prompts, single shot | Workload pack: multi-turn replay, 512/2K/8K/32K prompt TTFT, decode at depth (`llama-bench -d`) | 1 |
| G4 | Prompt/conversation cache: checkpoints, prefix pinning, parking in host RAM | Never measured | llama-server prefix reuse (`--cache-reuse`, slot save/restore, host prompt cache if the pin has it) measured on the G3 multi-turn pack; this is the TTFT lever | 2 |
| G5 | `--calibrate`: sweeps host-dependent knobs (pcie-frac, workers, adapt rate), keeps one only if >3% faster, remembers per PC+model | T-CAL measures constants only; knobs stay at defaults | Runtime autotuner over `-t`, `-ub/-b`, `--moe-cache-cpu-share`, cache size, `--cpu-mask/--prio`, with an A/A noise floor and a keep-if-≥3% rule | 2 |
| G6 | Per-miss routing: upload over PCIe vs compute on CPU (`--pcie-frac`, auto from CPU speed) | Static vs cache as a binary choice; C3 arm (cpu-share 0.9) is the first probe | Planner lever for the miss split, fed by CAL2 H2D and CPU GB/s | 2 |
| G7 | Router lookahead prefetch: next-layer experts predicted, with prefetch accuracy scored (`LOOKAHEAD_STATS`) | Routing traces exist; never scored for predictability | Offline lookahead-accuracy tool on T-QRT traces. This decides whether prefetch can hide PCIe misses before anyone writes a kernel | 2 |
| G8 | Adaptive cache policy plus offline replay (`replay_cache_policy.py`, adapt-every/swaps/decay) | T-POL (LRU/SLRU/ClassLRU replay) is in review | Add decay/swap-rate policies and validate replay against the engine `-lv 4` hit rate | 3 |
| G9 | KV levers: k8v4, Hadamard-rotated q4 KV, KV streaming (resident window in VRAM, rest in RAM), kv-grow (KV ↔ expert cache trade) | q8_0 KV fix (D033); KV types; `--no-kv-offload` never tried | Measure K/V asymmetric types and `-nkvo` at long context as levers; planner trades KV VRAM against expert slots | 2 |
| G10 | Lossy, cache-aware routing: `ROUTE_TAIL_SKIP` (skip low-rank missed experts, **on by default and it changes accuracy**), `ROUTE_PRIOR` (bias the router to resident experts) | Dynamic skipping is listed only as "research" | Engine patch plus a KLD/agreement gate. Strata shows why the gate matters: its default speedup silently costs accuracy | 3 |
| G11 | Batch-shape determinism: drafting/cache state changes greedy text (1-token vs multi-token kernels), with documented knobs for bit-exact A/B | D043 E2/E4 require **text identity**, which can fail on a lossless spec because verify batches use different kernels | Batch-invariance probe (same prompt, ub=1 vs n). Fall back to KLD/next-token agreement as the spec gate | 1 |
| G12 | Quality report: next-token agreement vs reference, "where the reference was sure", per task class, 5-token KL | KLD vs bf16 (Granite); no Qwen reference | Agreement@sure and per-task breakdown added to the verdict tool; Qwen reference logits (existing GAP §7) | 2 |
| G13 | Telemetry: `/metrics` with tier counters, hit_rate, pcie_share, drafts offered/accepted, per-stage decode timing | Parsed per experiment (`-lv 4` grep, draft_n by hand) | One telemetry parser → result record fields (hit rate, draft accept, split ms); engagement checks become automatic | 2 |
| G14 | Spec gating by measured acceptance × cost (prompt lookup only "where it pays"); MTP + lookup combined | ngram-mod is a WIN, but gated by hand (D042); E4 MTP pending | Workload-aware spec lever using T-SPECM's expert-union model plus a live acceptance threshold | 2 |
| G15 | CPU-pool placement: worker count, affinity, host-thread core, NUMA | Default threads always; 3700X is 2×CCX | Thread/affinity sweep (part of G5) | 3 |
| G16 | In-layer concurrent CPU+GPU expert compute via doorbells, without scheduler splits | Hybrid rejected (D030/31; QRT needs ~54 µs handoff vs 136–199 µs measured) | Handoff-floor microbench (pinned-flag doorbell round trip). It tells us whether the no-go is a llama.cpp limit or a physical one | 3 |
| G17 | Hybrid-attention models (DeltaNet/GDN recurrent state) | `inspect_model` assumes full-attention KV | State-size-aware inspector (check Qwen3.6 metadata when the download lands) | 2 |
| G18 | Concurrent requests (`parallel`): expert reads amortised across streams | Single-stream only | Throughput-vs-latency bench (`-np`, concurrent clients); low priority for local use | 4 |

Not adopted: Strata's "experimental speed projection" is a refusal-direction control vector. It is a safety removal, not an inference optimisation, so it is out of scope.
'''
marker='## Build next (ranked)'
t=t.replace(marker, sec.strip()+'\n\n'+marker,1)
p.write_text(t)
EOF
grep -c '^| G' TOOLKIT.md

What correlates and what doesn't

Strong, usable relationships

  • 1/decode is linear in bytes moved off the GPU. On Qwen each CPU layer adds 0.757 ms, which is about 30 GB/s, and the line holds from K=8 to K=48 (D039).
  • VRAM is linear in K: about 347 MiB per Qwen layer and 27 MiB per Granite layer. Planner MiB error is under 0.3%.
  • Cache hit rate decides cache vs static. Upload-mode cache wins when held-out coverage is about 70% or higher. CPU-share removes most of the miss penalty, so it wins much lower.
  • Expert size × handoff cost decides granularity. Crossover = fixed cost / per-byte cost (D031).
  • Paired KLD tracks quality where unpaired PPL can't (stderr 0.0015 vs 0.37).
  • imatrix → lower KLD at every bit width (−33% at 4-bit, −13% at 3-bit).
  • Copy-heavy text → speculation acceptance. Rewrite and repeat prompts give 2.4–3×; chat gives none.
  • Routing locality ranks code > prose > chat on both Granite and Qwen traces.

Weak, misleading or absent

  • Fewer bits ≠ faster on CPU. Q3_K unpacking is compute-bound on AVX2, so 3-bit was only +1.5%.
  • Greedy text identity ≠ quality. Every placement changes the text. The same config can even change it between runs (62290c73 vs 77a3045a).
  • Harness speedups ≠ integrated speedups. The integrated graph pays per-layer fixed costs (D030).
  • Proxy-model results ≠ target results. Granite results flipped on Qwen twice (D022, the planner).
  • Kernel count ≠ bandwidth. 40–46% of kernel time is in tiny kernels at under 1% DRAM.
  • Cache-policy choice barely matters. LRU, SLRU and ClassLRU are within 2 points. Budget and miss handling matter far more.
  • Profiled time ≠ real time. Node tracing inflates gaps 3×, and ncu serialises kernels.
  • Identical bytes in a different file vary ±5%, so effects under 5% need A/A and alternation.
  • A reported hit rate can mislead (Strata: PCIe-served experts are not counted).

Structure vs flexibility

The campaign settled into two speeds. Unfrozen screens find things quickly, and frozen protocols decide whether to accept them. Each side caught errors the other would have missed.

Where structure paid off

  • The frozen quiet-host rerun retracted PAP (+9.8% → +1.5%) before it reached the factory.
  • The plan → measure loop caught the planner's 5% decode optimism on its first run.
  • Engagement checks caught static-hot never running. Without them it would have been timed as "no gain".
  • run_ref image identity fixed the wrong-image-id bug (D016).
  • Plausibility guards rejected 1384 GB/s before it fed the planner.
  • The A/A interference check let downloads run during timing at a measured 0.2% cost.
  • Recorded ops made every number here traceable to a command.

Where flexibility paid off

  • An hour-long unfrozen screen found the +38% cache win that overturned D022.
  • Research intake found ngram-mod (2.4–3× for free) and upstream cpu-share, which flipped 4 GB tonight.
  • Rebasing to upstream (519 commits) brought levers we would have spent days building.
  • bpftrace and perf were set up ad hoc in minutes and confirmed the CPU-layer cost by a second method.
  • Delegating to Codex let six tools run in parallel (POL, SPECM, PROFW, CAL2, VER, PL4).

Where structure cost too much

  • Hand-written test JSON per experiment led to a scripted runner instead of bin/lab.
  • A text-identity criterion in E2/E4 may reject lossless speculation (G11).
  • Mocked fixtures passed tests and failed on real output 3 times.
  • A wait-gate meant to keep the host quiet deadlocked the overnight chain.

Rule of thumb: be strict about identity, provenance, engagement, noise floors and acceptance criteria. Be flexible about where ideas come from, which engine is the base, and how a screen is run. Of the 43 notes, about 6 are infra bugs, 4 are user directives, 6 are frozen protocols and about 27 are results. Every result that later reversed came from a proxy model, a harness or a noisy window.

Expected vs unexpected

Went as expected

  • Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound wherever experts live.
  • Quantization quality ordering: Q8 ≈ lossless, 4-bit costs a little, 2-bit collapses.
  • CUDA graphs help (4.2%). Small-kernel fusion has headroom.
  • KV q8_0 halves KV cost at no quality cost once fixed.
  • Speculation gains depend on the workload.

Surprised us

  • The expert cache flipped from loser (Granite) to winner (Qwen), then won at 4 GB too once misses could stay on the CPU.
  • Per-layer handoff, not bytes, dominated Granite decode (GPU idle 80%).
  • 3-bit experts were barely faster on the CPU.
  • Qwen3 thinking mode silently disabled n-gram drafting.
  • The handoff estimate varies 4× depending on the method (52–199 µs).
  • Zen 2 exposes no DRAM counters to perf on this kernel.
  • The same config gave different greedy text between runs.
  • Provider refusals were triggered by crash/debug wording in a Codex brief.

Rough base rates

  • Of 23 written predictions: 8 confirmed, 4 magnitude off, 4 reversed, 7 silent failures.
  • Anything that transfers from proxy to target: about half reversed or were off by more than 2×.
  • First-run tooling on real output: about 1 in 2 needed a fix (CAL1, CAL2, T-CAL CPU probe, ngram, chain).
  • Same-model, in-range predictions: almost always within 10%.

Methodologies

Measurement

  • Pre-register, then measure. Freeze the protocol before results exist.
  • A/A first to get the noise floor, then matched A/B in ABBA order with medians.
  • Quiet host: no compiles, Codex runs or unthrottled downloads. Check it per arm and label the arm otherwise.
  • Rerun anything provisional that came from a noisy window.
  • Profile with a perturbation check against unprofiled timing.
  • Sample peak VRAM from outside the process (nvidia-smi every 0.5 s).

Correctness

  • Engagement before timing: prove the code path ran with counters or log lines.
  • Text identity for exact rewrites. KLD/PPL for anything numerical, including placement.
  • Paired KLD vs reference logits. Never unpaired PPL alone.
  • test-backend-ops for every patched op.
  • Sort every claim into a category: full-engine gain, representation trade-off, placement-only, or failed.

Modeling and transfer

  • Label each result transferable or proxy-only. Proxy results are hypotheses on the target.
  • Predict from bytes and measured constants, and say "extrapolated" outside the calibration range.
  • Report fixed per-layer cost next to per-byte cost.
  • Plausibility guards on every microbenchmark (no faster-than-peak numbers).
  • Leave one model out before trusting a fit.

Process and delegation

  • Opus orchestrates. Codex does bounded work from written assignments and is reviewed against real records.
  • Capture real tool output as fixtures. Mocks hide real failures.
  • Every action goes through run_op, so every number has a command.
  • Research intake → smallest probe → indicative screen → frozen experiment → planner lever.
  • Avoid pgrep/pkill patterns that can match their own command line.

MoE Inference Factory Ledger

Everything built, found, ruled out and still missing in the factory that takes an MoE model, inspects it and the host, and produces an engine configuration that runs the model in much less memory at the same accuracy. It covers 43 decision notes, about 22 components, 7 skills, 300 artifact runs and one overnight experiment that is still running.

Hosts: x86 (Ryzen 7 3700X, DDR4 dual channel, RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, PCIe 4.0) · Jetson Orin Nano (no reply yet). Models: Granite-3.1-1B-A400M (proxy 1), Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (proxy 2), REAP-15B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MTP (downloading).
